actual_source_passage_consultation.body:
## Definition

Fix a target population with probability law $P$, a real outcome, and a nonempty countable discrete set $\mathcal A$ of treatment versions. A treatment version $a\in\mathcal A$ is a specified intervention protocol, not just a treatment label. The **potential outcome** $Y^a$ is the real random variable giving the outcome for a unit in the target population under version $a$. Write $A$ for the observed treatment assignment or receipt, with values in $\mathcal A$, and $Y$ for the observed outcome. The **observed potential outcome** is the measurable random variable

$$Y^A=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}\mathbf 1_{\{A=a\}}Y^a,$$

where the countable sum has at most one nonzero summand at each sample point. **Consistency** is the assumption $Y=Y^A$ $P$-almost surely. It links the observed outcome to the potential outcome for the received version; it does not assert that treatment assignment is unconfounded.

The **full-data law** is the joint law of the potential-outcome family, $A$, any baseline covariate random element $L$, and $Y$. The **observed-data law** is its marginal law of $(A,L,Y)$. A target population, outcome, intervention protocol, and contrast must be fixed before the associated causal target is specified. If interference between units matters, the version or treatment regime must include the relevant assignment or exposure of other units; the notation $Y^a$ by itself does not assert no interference.

## Definition

In a fixed target population with two specified treatment versions $0$ and $1$ and integrable potential outcomes $Y^0,Y^1$ from [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]], the **average treatment effect (ATE)** is the target-population mean contrast $E[Y^1-Y^0]$. For a baseline covariate random element $L$, the **conditional average treatment effect (CATE) given $L$** is the conditional-expectation almost-sure class

$$E[Y^1-Y^0\mid\sigma(L)],$$

using the conditional-expectation convention of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]] under the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Thus a CATE is determined only up to equality almost surely under the target law of $L$; a pointwise value at a null covariate value is not specified by this definition. The ATE is the mean of the individual contrast, not an assertion that both potential outcomes are observed for any unit.

## Definition

Let $A$ take values in a countable discrete set on a target probability space, and let $L$ be the baseline covariate random element. For a treatment value $a$ of interest, the conditional treatment probability is the almost-sure class

$$e_a=E[\mathbf 1_{\{A=a\}}\mid\sigma(L)],$$

using the conditional-expectation convention of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]] under the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. **Positivity for $a$ on the target population** means both $P(A=a)>0$ and $e_a>0$ almost surely under the target law of $L$. Positivity for a contrast is required at every treatment value in that contrast.

The almost-sure condition is relative to the target population: values of $L$ with zero target probability impose no condition. Strict positivity does not mean that $e_a$ is bounded away from zero. The marginal condition makes the observed treatment-stratum law $P(\,\cdot\mid A=a)$ available.

## Definition

Let $A$ be the observed treatment assignment, $L$ a baseline covariate random element, and $(Y^a)_{a\in\mathcal A}$ the potential-outcome family of [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]. **Conditional exchangeability given $L$** means

$$\sigma(Y^a:a\in\mathcal A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(A)\mid\sigma(L),$$

where conditional independence is the bounded-measurable-function factorization of [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]] under the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Each fixed $Y^a$ is then conditionally independent of $A$ given $L$ by measurable-map preservation in [[lem-conditional-independence-equivalences-and-preservation]]. This is a full-data assumption; the observed distribution alone does not establish it.

## Statement

Assume the [[def-axiom-of-choice]] for the conditional-expectation classes. Let $U$ be a real integrable random variable, let $Z$ be a random element, and let $\mathcal G$ be a sub-sigma-algebra. If $U$ and $Z$ are conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$ in the bounded-function sense of [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]], then for every bounded measurable real function $h$ on the state space of $Z$,

$$E[U h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]=E[U\mid\mathcal G]E[h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{almost surely}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, $U\in L^1(P)$, a random element $Z$, a sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G$, and $U\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed for the conditional-expectation classes used in this lemma. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Conditional independence is the bounded-product conditional-expectation identity. [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]

[F2] Conditional-expectation notation denotes the almost-sure class of versions, which exists under the stated Choice assumption. [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]

[F3] Under Choice, conditional expectation contracts every $L^p$ norm for $1\le p\le\infty$, in particular $L^1$ and $L^\infty$. [[cor-conditional-lp-contraction]]

## Proof

1.1 For each integer $n\ge1$, let $T_n(u)=\max(-n,\min(u,n))$. The functions $T_n(U)$ and $h(Z)$ are bounded and measurable, so [F1] gives the identity $E[T_n(U)h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]=E[T_n(U)\mid\mathcal G]E[h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]$ of the classes in [F2]. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Since $U\in L^1$, $T_n(U)\to U$ in $L^1$; boundedness of $h$ gives $T_n(U)h(Z)\to Uh(Z)$ in $L^1$. By [F3], the conditional expectations on the left converge in $L^1$ to $E[Uh(Z)\mid\mathcal G]$, and $E[T_n(U)\mid\mathcal G]\to E[U\mid\mathcal G]$ in $L^1$. Also $|E[h(Z)\mid\mathcal G]|\le\|h\|_\infty$ almost surely by [F3], so multiplication by this factor preserves that $L^1$ convergence. Taking the $L^1$ limits in step 1.1 proves the stated identity of almost-sure classes. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

actual_source_passage_consultation.body:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal A$ be a countable discrete set containing treatment versions $0$ and $1$. On a full-data probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, let $A$ take values in $\mathcal A$, let $L$ take values in a standard-Borel space $\mathcal L$ ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), let $Y$ be the observed real outcome, and let $(Y^b)_{b\in\mathcal A}$ be the potential outcomes of [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]. For each treatment value $a$ under consideration, assume $Y^a\in L^1(P)$, consistency $Y=Y^A$ almost surely, conditional exchangeability $\sigma(Y^b:b\in\mathcal A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(A)\mid\sigma(L)$, and positivity $P(A=a)>0$ and $E[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}\mid\sigma(L)]>0$ almost surely. These are assumptions on the full-data law; Choice is required for the stated conditional-expectation classes and regular conditional distributions.

Write $P_L(B)=P(L\in B)$ for the target-population law of $L$. For such an $a$, define the observed treatment-stratum law $P_a(C)=P(C\cap\{A=a\})/P(A=a)$. Under $P_a$, let $K_a(l,dy)$ be a regular conditional law of $Y$ given the standard-Borel random element $L$, and put $m_a(l)=\int y\,K_a(l,dy)$ wherever the absolute integral is finite, with value $0$ on the exceptional set. The suppliers [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]], [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]], [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]], and [[thm-conditional-integration-through-a-regular-conditional-law]] give this construction. Then $m_a$ is $P_L$-integrable and is uniquely determined $P_L$-almost everywhere by the observed-data law, and

$$E_P[Y^a]=\int_{\mathcal L}m_a(l)\,P_L(dl).$$

If $L$ is countably discrete, this is

$$E_P[Y^a]=\sum_{l:P(L=l)>0}E_P[Y\mid A=a,L=l]P(L=l).$$

In this sum, $E[Y\mid A=a,L=l]$ denotes $E[Y\mathbf1_{\{A=a,L=l\}}]/P(A=a,L=l)$, whose denominator is positive for each displayed atom.

For the binary contrast, both treatment levels must satisfy positivity. The CATE is then represented $P_L$-almost everywhere by $m_1-m_0$, and the ATE is $\int(m_1-m_0)\,dP_L$. In the model whose parameters are all full-data laws satisfying these assumptions and whose observation map sends a full-data law to its $(A,L,Y)$ marginal, each $E[Y^a]$ is identifiable in the sense of [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]: it is constant over full-data laws with the same observed-data law.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Choice; a full-data probability law; countable discrete treatment versions; a standard-Borel covariate $L$; integrable potential outcomes for the treatment values considered; consistency; conditional exchangeability; and positivity.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed. It supplies the conditional-expectation classes and standard-Borel regular conditional distributions used below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Potential outcomes are indexed by specified treatment versions, the observed outcome is $Y^A$, and consistency is $Y=Y^A$ almost surely. [[def-potential-outcomes-and-consistency]]

[F2] Conditional exchangeability means the sigma-algebra generated by the potential-outcome family is conditionally independent of the treatment sigma-algebra given $\sigma(L)$. [[def-conditional-exchangeability-of-potential-outcomes]]

[F3] For each treatment $a$ under consideration, $P(A=a)>0$ and $E[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}\mid\sigma(L)]>0$ almost surely under the target law. [[def-positivity-for-discrete-treatment]]

[F4] The ATE is $E[Y^1-Y^0]$, and the CATE is the conditional-expectation class $E[Y^1-Y^0\mid\sigma(L)]$. [[def-causal-average-treatment-effects]]

[F5] A conditional-expectation version is an integrable $\sigma(L)$-measurable function satisfying the defining event-integral identities; under Choice its unique almost-sure class is available. [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]], [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]

[F6] Conditional independence of an integrable real variable and a random element extends the bounded-product identity to any bounded measurable function of that random element. [[lem-conditional-independence-integrable-factorization]]

[F7] Under Choice, a real-valued random element has a regular conditional distribution given any sub-sigma-algebra. [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]]

[F8] For standard-Borel $L$, a regular conditional distribution given $\sigma(L)$ factors through an everywhere probability kernel on the value space of $L$; this is the conditional law given $L$. [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]], [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]

[F9] Integrating the identity function against that conditional law, with zero fill where the absolute integral is infinite, gives a real conditional-expectation version under $P_a$. [[thm-conditional-integration-through-a-regular-conditional-law]]

[F10] Conditional-expectation versions with the same defining event integrals agree almost surely. [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]

[F11] A finite $\sigma(L)$-measurable factor can be taken out of conditional expectation when the products are integrable. [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]]

[F12] Conditional expectation preserves ordinary expectation and is the tower of nested conditional expectations. [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]], [[thm-tower-property-of-conditional-expectation]]

[F13] The expectation of a measurable function of a random element is its integral against that random element's law. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

[F14] An estimand is identifiable when it is constant on parameter values with the same observed sampling law. [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** Construct each observed treatment-stratum law, transport its conditional mean to the target covariate law by exchangeability and positivity, and then apply the definition of identifiability.

1.1 Fix a treatment value $a$ satisfying the hypotheses, write $e_a=E[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}\mid\sigma(L)]$, and define $P_a(C)=P(C\cap\{A=a\})/P(A=a)$. For every Borel $B\subseteq\mathcal L$, the defining event-integral identity for $e_a$ gives $P_a(L\in B)=E_P[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}e_a]/P(A=a)$. [A1, F3, F5, construct]

1.2 Under $P_a$, $Y$ is integrable because $Y=Y^a$ on $\{A=a\}$ by consistency and $E_{P_a}|Y|=E_P[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}|Y^a|]/P(A=a)\le E_P|Y^a|/P(A=a)$. By [A1, F7, F8], choose a conditional law $K_a(l,dy)$ of $Y$ given $L$ under $P_a$; [F9] makes its zero-filled integral $m_a(L)$ a real integrable version of $E_{P_a}[Y\mid\sigma(L)]$. [A1, F1, F7, F8, F9]

1.3 Put $v_a=E_P[Y^a\mid\sigma(L)]$. Conditional independence in [F2], applied to the coordinate $Y^a$ and the bounded indicator $\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}$, together with [F6], gives $E_P[\mathbf1_{\{A=a\}}Y^a\mid\sigma(L)]=e_a v_a$ almost surely. [A1, F2, F3, F6]

2.1 The covariate laws $P_{a,L}$ and $P_L$ are equivalent. Indeed, $P_L(B)=0$ makes the numerator in step 1.1 zero. Conversely, if $P_L(B)>0$, positivity gives $P(L\in B,e_a>0)>0$; since $\{e_a>0\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{e_a\ge1/n\}$ up to a null set, some $n$ has $P(L\in B,e_a\ge1/n)>0$, so the numerator is positive. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

2.2 For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal L)$, the defining event integrals of $m_a(L)$ under $P_a$, consistency [F1], step 1.3, and the take-out rule [F11] give $E_{P_a}[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}m_a(L)]=E_{P_a}[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}Y]=E_{P_a}[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}Y^a]=E_{P_a}[\mathbf1_{\{L\in B\}}v_a]$. [F1, F9, F11, step 1.3]

3.1 Both $m_a(L)$ and $v_a$ are $\sigma(L)$-measurable integrable versions under $P_a$ with the same event integrals for $Y$. Uniqueness [F10] gives $m_a(L)=v_a$ $P_a$-almost surely. Step 2.1 transfers this equality to $P_L$-almost every covariate value, so the integral in the statement is finite and independent of the conditional-law version and its null-set filler. [F9, F10, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 By [F12], $E_P[v_a]=E_P[Y^a]$. Since $m_a(L)=v_a$ $P$-almost surely on the target covariate law by step 3.1, the change-of-variables identity [F13] yields $\int m_a(l)P_L(dl)=E_P[Y^a]$. [F12, F13, step 3.1]

5.1 If $L$ is countably discrete, positivity implies $P(A=a,L=l)>0$ for every atom $l$ with $P(L=l)>0$, so the conditional-mean definition in the statement and the version identity [F9] give $m_a(l)=E[Y\mid A=a,L=l]$ there. Splitting the integral in step 4.1 over the countable support proves the displayed sum; its absolute convergence follows from the integrability of $v_a$. For $a=0,1$, linearity of conditional expectation [F12] gives the CATE version $m_1(L)-m_0(L),$ and subtraction of the two mean identities gives the ATE formula. Equal observed-data laws give the same $P_L$, stratum laws $P_a$, and $P_a$ conditional-mean classes; step 2.1 makes these classes unique on the target support. Hence [F14] identifies each $E[Y^a]$ and the ATE. [F3, F4, F9, F10, F12, F13, F14, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

This theorem is for discrete treatment values. For continuous $A$, conditional-law versions are uniquely determined only $P_A$-almost everywhere: any two regular conditional laws agree outside a single conditioning-law null set by [[lem-simultaneous-ae-uniqueness-of-regular-conditional-distributions]], and factoring through $A$ transfers that qualification to $P_A$. The theorem asserts no pointwise causal effect at a $P_A$-null value; a specified version and any continuity or smoothness assumptions need a separate proof. Conditional exchangeability is generally untestable from the observed law. If positivity fails on a target stratum, that stratum's counterfactual mean is unsupported by the observed treatment data; the theorem does not identify the full target by this formula.

## Definition

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

## Definition

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

## Definition

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

## Statement

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integrable functions $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$.

[L1] Real and complex integrability, together with the decomposition into positive and negative parts and into real and imaginary parts, is defined in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

[L2] The nonnegative integral is additive ([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

[L3] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[L4] Sums and real scalar multiples of measurable real-valued functions are measurable ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First treat real-valued $f,g$ and put $h:=f+g$. By [L4], the function $h$ is measurable. Also $$h^+\le f^++g^+,\qquad h^-\le f^-+g^-,$$ so [L2] and [L3] give $$\int h^+\,d\mu\le\int f^+\,d\mu+\int g^+\,d\mu<+\infty,\qquad \int h^-\,d\mu\le\int f^-\,d\mu+\int g^-\,d\mu<+\infty.$$ Hence $h$ is integrable. Since $$h^++f^-+g^-=h^-+f^++g^+,$$ another application of [L2] yields $$\int h^+\,d\mu+\int f^-\,d\mu+\int g^-\,d\mu =\int h^-\,d\mu+\int f^+\,d\mu+\int g^+\,d\mu,$$ which rearranges to $$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$ [L1, L2, L3, L4, algebra]

1.2 Now let $c\in\mathbb R$ and let $f$ be real-valued. By [L4], $cf$ is measurable. If $c\ge0$, then $$(cf)^+=cf^+,\qquad (cf)^-=cf^-;$$ if $c<0$, then $$(cf)^+=(-c)f^-,\qquad (cf)^-=(-c)f^+.$$ In both cases [L3] shows that $cf$ is integrable and that $$\int(cf)\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu.$$ [L1, L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 Let $h=u+iv\in L^1(\mu)$ and $\gamma=a+ib\in\mathbb C$. Then $$\gamma h=(au-bv)+i(av+bu).$$ The real-valued functions $au-bv$ and $av+bu$ are integrable by steps 1.1 and 1.2, and their real-linear integral formulas combine into $$\int(\gamma h)\,d\mu=\gamma\int h\,d\mu.$$ Writing $\alpha f=h_1+ik_1$ and $\beta g=h_2+ik_2$ with real-valued integrable $h_j,k_j$, step 1.1 gives $$\int(\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu =\int(h_1+h_2)\,d\mu+i\int(k_1+k_2)\,d\mu =\int h_1\,d\mu+i\int k_1\,d\mu+\int h_2\,d\mu+i\int k_2\,d\mu =\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu.$$ [L1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Independent random elements $X_i$ and measurable maps $g_i$ as in the Statement.

[L1] Measurable outer maps preserve measurability under composition. ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]])

[L2] Independence of random elements is equivalent to the rectangle criterion. ([[thm-rectangle-criterion-for-independent-random-elements]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], each composite $g_i\circ X_i$ is again a random element. [given, L1]

1.2 Fix a finite list of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$ and measurable sets $C_k\in\mathcal T_{i_k}$. Then $g_{i_k}^{-1}(C_k)\in\Sigma_{i_k}$ for every $k$, so [L2] applied to the independent family $(X_i)$ gives $$\mathbb P(g_{i_0}(X_{i_0})\in C_0,\dots,g_{i_{n-1}}(X_{i_{n-1}})\in C_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(g_{i_k}(X_{i_k})\in C_k).$$ [given, L2]

2.1 Step 1.2 is exactly the rectangle criterion for the family $(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$, so [L2] shows that this family is independent. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Independent real random variables $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ and Borel measurable functions $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$.

[L1] Measurable coordinatewise functions preserve independence. ([[lem-measurable-functions-preserve-independence]])

[L2] Independent random elements have product joint law. ([[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]])

[L3] Expectation is integration against the law after a measurable change of variables. ([[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]])

[L4] Tonelli evaluates nonnegative product-measurable integrands on a sigma-finite product space. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[L5] Fubini evaluates absolutely integrable product-measurable integrands on a sigma-finite product space. ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[L6] On a product measurable space, coordinate projections are measurable, and finite sums and products of measurable real-valued functions remain measurable. ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]])

[L7] A nonnegative measurable function has zero integral exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere ([[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]).

[L8] Increasing nonnegative measurable functions pass to the limit under the integral ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Put $Y_i:=g_i(X_i)$. By [L1], the family $Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1}$ is independent. On $\mathbb R^n$ with the finite product sigma-algebra, each coordinate projection $\pi_i$ is measurable because $\pi_i^{-1}(B)=\mathbb R^i\times B\times\mathbb R^{n-1-i}$ is a measurable rectangle. Repeated use of [L6] therefore makes the product map $m(y_0,\dots,y_{n-1})=\prod_{i<n}y_i$ measurable. [L1, L6]

2.1 Assume each $g_i$ is nonnegative. If some $\mathbb E[g_j(X_j)]=0$, [L7] gives $Y_j=0$ almost surely. The finite product $\prod_iY_i$ is then zero almost surely, so [L7] gives expectation zero, agreeing with the Statement's explicit zero-factor convention even if another expectation is infinite. [step 1.1, L7]

2.2 Otherwise every $\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$ is positive (possibly infinite). Let $\mu_i$ be the law of $Y_i$ and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mu_i$. By [L2], the joint law of $Y=(Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1})$ is $\mu$. For each integer $k\ge1$, put $Y_i^{(k)}=Y_i\wedge k$. The finite product $\prod_iY_i^{(k)}$ is bounded, so [L3] and repeated [L4] give $\mathbb E[\prod_iY_i^{(k)}]=\prod_i\mathbb E[Y_i^{(k)}]$ with only finite factors. As $k\uparrow\infty$, the products increase pointwise to $\prod_iY_i$; [L8] passes the limit through the left integral and each factor on the right. Since all limiting factors are strictly positive, the finite product of their increasing approximants tends to their ordinary extended product without an indeterminate zero-times-infinity expression. [step 1.1, L2, L3, L4, L8]

3.1 Now assume every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable. Applying steps 2.1–2.2 to the nonnegative functions $|g_i|$ gives $\mathbb E[\prod_{i<n}|g_i(X_i)|]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[|g_i(X_i)|]<\infty$. So $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable. [step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 Let $\mu_i$ be the law of $Y_i=g_i(X_i)$ and $\mu=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mu_i$ as in step 2.2. Step 3.1 shows that the product map $m$ is $\mu$-integrable. By [L2], [L3], and repeated use of [L5], $\mathbb E[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)]=\int_{\mathbb R^n}m\,d\mu=\prod_{i<n}\int_{\mathbb R}y\,d\mu_i=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, L2, L3, L5]

5.1 Steps 2.1–2.2 prove the nonnegative case, and step 4.1 proves the integrable case. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if $f+g$ is pointwise defined, then $f+g$ is measurable;
4. with the convention of
   [[rem-zero-times-infinity-convention-for-pointwise-products]], the pointwise
   product $fg$ is measurable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A measurable space $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and measurable functions $f,g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$.

[L1] Extended-real measurability is equivalent to measurability of the threshold sets $\{h>a\}$. ([[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]])

[L2] The positive and negative parts are $h^+ = \max(h,0)$ and $h^- = \max(-h,0)$. ([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]])

[A1] In this proof, the pointwise product uses the page convention $0 \cdot (+\infty)=0 \cdot (-\infty)=0$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Scalar multiples are measurable. If $c>0$, then $\{cf>a\}=\{f>a/c\}$; if $c<0$, then $\{cf>a\}=\{f<a/c\}$; and if $c=0$, the function is constant. So [L1] gives measurability of $cf$, and in particular of $-f$. [given, L1]

2.1 The threshold identities $$\{\max(f,g)>a\} = \{f>a\} \cup \{g>a\},\qquad \{\min(f,g)>a\} = \{f>a\} \cap \{g>a\}$$ show via [L1] that $\max(f,g)$ and $\min(f,g)$ are measurable. By [L2], this proves measurability of $f^+$ and $f^-$; replacing $g$ by $-f$ also gives $|f|=\max(f,-f)$. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

3.1 Assume $f+g$ is pointwise defined. For every real $a$, $$\{f+g>a\} = \bigcup_{q \in \mathbb{Q}} \big(\{f>q\} \cap \{g>a-q\}\big).$$ The inclusion from right to left is immediate. For the converse, if $f(x)+g(x)>a$ then either $f(x)=+\infty$, in which case any rational $q>a-g(x)$ works, or $f(x)$ is finite and one may choose a rational $q$ with $a-g(x)<q<f(x)$. Thus [L1] gives measurability of $f+g$. [step 2.1, L1]

4.1 Suppose first that $u,v : X \to [0,+\infty]$ are nonnegative and measurable. If $a<0$, then $\{uv>a\}=X$. If $a \ge 0$, then $$\{uv>a\} = \bigcup_{q \in \mathbb{Q},\, q>0} \big(\{u>q\} \cap \{v>a/q\}\big).$$ Again the inclusion from right to left is immediate. For the converse, if $u(x)v(x)>a$, choose a rational $q$ with $0<q<u(x)$ and $a/q<v(x)$; this is possible because either $u(x)$ is finite positive and the rationals are dense, or $u(x)=+\infty$, in which case any sufficiently large positive rational works. Hence nonnegative products are measurable by [L1]. [step 3.1, L1, A1]

5.1 For general measurable $f$ and $g$, step 2.1 gives measurable nonnegative functions $f^+,f^-,g^+,g^-$. By step 4.1 the four products $f^+g^+, f^-g^-, f^+g^-, f^-g^+$ are measurable. Put $$h_+ := f^+g^+ + f^-g^-,\qquad h_- := f^+g^- + f^-g^+.$$ At each point, at least one of $h_+$ and $h_-$ is zero, because at least one of $f^+,f^-$ and at least one of $g^+,g^-$ is zero. So the difference $h_+ - h_-$ is pointwise defined without the forbidden $\infty-\infty$ form, and step 3.1 makes it measurable. By the usual sign decomposition, $h_+ - h_- = fg$, with the convention [A1] at the $0 \cdot \infty$ points. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, L2, A1]

6.1 Steps 1.1 through 5.1 prove all four claims. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Assumption (IV1) says we get to observe the counterfactuals that correspond to the observed value of the instrument
\(Z\)

For the outcome, we only get to observe the counterfactual outcome

.
This is the case in the randomized encouragement design above about smoking where the researcher only has two interventions: the encouragement to quit smoking or the usual care.
Note that SUTVA also implies two “mini” assumptions about no multiple versions of treatment and no interference.
Assumption (IV2) says that the instrument (i.e.
\(Z\)

This is the case in the randomized encouragement design about smoking where the encouragement intervention (i.e.,
\(Z\)

Assumption (IV3) says that all values of the instrument have a non-zero probability of being realized.
This is also the case in the randomized encouragement design above where some mothers were randomized to the encouragement intervention while other mothers were randomized to the usual care.
In short, (IV1)-(IV3) are conceptually identical to (A1)-(A3) where
\(Z\)
is replaced by
\(A\)
.

Monotonicity-Based IV Assumptions
Under a randomized encouragement design, we can formalize the assumptions about the instrument
\(Z\)
. This is broadly referred to as “monotonicity-based” IV assumptions.
(IV4, Instrument relevance):
\(\mathbb{E}[A(1) - A(0)] \neq 0\)

for all
\(a\)

\(z=1\)
and
\(z=0\)

\(a\)

\(X\)
If pre-instrument covariates
\(X\)
are present and are necessary to justify (IV1)-(IV3), for instance the investigator ran a stratified randomized encouragement design, it’s likely the case that we need to modify (IV4)-(IV6) to incorporate

Proof of Identification of the LATE with (IV1)-(IV6)
We will show that under (IV1)-(IV6), we have
\[\begin{align*} {\rm LATE} &= \frac{\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=0]}{\mathbb{E}[A \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[A \mid Z=0] } \end{align*}\]
We first begin with the numerator of the above ratio.
\[\begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=1] \\ =& \mathbb{E}[Z Y(A(1),1) + (1-Z) Y(A(0),0) \mid Z=1] && \text{(IV1, SUTVA)} \\ =& \mathbb{E}[Y(A(1),1)\mid Z= 1] && \\ =& \mathbb{E}[Y(1,1)A(1) + Y(0,1)(1-A(1)) \mid Z=1] && \\ =& \mathbb{E}[Y(1,1)A(1) + Y(0,1)(1-A(1))] && \text{(IV2, Ignorable $Z$)} \\ =& \mathbb{E}[Y(1)A(1) + Y(0)(1-A(1))] && \text{(IV5, Exclusion restriction)} \end{align*}\]
Note that (IV3, Positivity of
\(Z\)
) is needed to ensure that the conditional expectation are well-defined. By a similar argument, we have
\(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=0] = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)A(0) + Y(0)(1-A(0))]\)
.
Second, we take the difference between the two expectations of
\(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=1]\)
and
\(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z= 0]\)
.
\[\begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=0] \\ =& \mathbb{E}[ \{Y(1)A(1) + Y(0)(1-A(1))\} - \{Y(1)A(0) + Y(0)(1-A(0))\}] \\ =&\mathbb{E}[Y(1)\{A(1) - A(0)\} - Y(0)\{A(1) - A(0)\}] \\ =&\mathbb{E}[\{Y(1) - Y(0)\}\{A(1) - A(0)\}] \\ =& \mathbb{E}[\{Y(1) - Y(0)\} I(A(1) - A(0) = 1) + \{Y(1) - Y(0)\} I(A(1) - A(0) = -1) ] \\ =&\mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) | A(1) - A(0) = 1] \mathbb{P}(A(1) - A(0) = 1) && \text{(IV6, Monotonicity)} \end{align*}\]
The last equality also uses the definition of conditional expectation.
Third, we can rewrite the denominator of the ratio above as follows:
\[\begin{align*} &\mathbb{E}[A \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[A \mid Z=0] \\ =&\mathbb{E}[A(1) - A(0)] && \text{(IV1)-(IV3)} \\ =&\mathbb{P}(A(1) - A(0) = 1) && \text{(IV6)}. \end{align*}\]
Finally, under (IV4, Instrument relevance), we can take the ratio of the two differences since the denominator of this ratio is non-zero:
\[\begin{align*} &\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z=0]}{\mathbb{E}[A \mid Z=1] - \mathbb{E}[A \mid Z=0] } \\ =& \frac{\mathbb{E}[ Y(1) - Y(0) | A(1) - A(0) = 1] \mathbb{P}(A(1) - A(0) = 1) }{\mathbb{P}(A(1) - A(0) = 1)} \\ =&\mathbb{E}[ Y(1) - Y(0) | A(1) - A(0) = 1] \end{align*}\]
Note

Chapter 16
INSTRUMENTAL VARIABLE ESTIMATION
The causal inference methods described so far in this book rely on a key untestable assumption: all variables needed
to adjust for confounding and selection bias have been identified and correctly measured. If this assumption is
incorrect—and it will always be to a certain extent—there will be residual bias in our causal estimates.
It turns out that there exist other methods that can validly estimate causal effects under an alternative set
of assumptions that do not require measuring all adjustment factors. Instrumental variable estimation is one of
those methods. Economists and other social scientists reading this book can breathe now. We are finally going to
describe a very common method in their fields, a method that is unlike any other we have discussed so far.
16.1 The three instrumental conditions
The causal diagram in Figure 16.1 depicts a randomized trial: Z is the ran-
domization assignment indicator (1: treatment, 0: placebo), A is an indicator
for receiving treatment (1: yes, 0: no) because not all participants adhere to
their assignment, Y the outcome, and U all factors (some unmeasured) that
affect both the outcome and the adherence. Because participants and their
doctors do not know whether the pill they are given is treatment or placebo,
they are said to be “blinded ” and the study is referred to as a double-blind
placebo-controlled randomized trial.
Suppose we want to consistently estimate the average causal effect of A on
Y . Whether we use IP weighting, standardization, g-estimation, stratification,
or matching, we need to correctly measure, and adjust for, variables that block

result in biased effect estimates if some of the necessary variables are unmea-

attempt to identify the average causal effect of A on Y in this randomized

an instrumental variable Z, or an instrument. A variable Z is an instrument
because it meets three instrumental conditions:
(i) Z is associated with A
(ii) Z does not affect Y except through its potential effect on A
(iii) Z and Y do not share causes
